---
name: ship-plan
description: "Land a reviewed plan as AGENTS.md's Landing section says: push it or open its pull request, tag and publish its release, close its issues"
---
Land the plan in `PLAN.md` the way this repository's Landing policy says: push its commits to the default branch or open its pull request, tag and publish its release, comment on and close its issue, and file its follow-ups as issues. Run it again at any time: each stage checks whether it is done and skips it, so a run that stopped partway, or a pull request that has merged since, carries on where it left off. Never force-push, rebase onto a moved default branch, move a tag, delete a tag `origin` has, or delete a release.

Extra instructions (may be empty): the request given after the command name

1. Read the state: run `pwsh -NoProfile -File .template/Get-PlanState.ps1` from the repository root. It prints `key: value` lines. Below, `<default>` is its `default` value, `<branch>` its `branch` and `<version>` its `release`. Stop and say what to run instead when `plan` is `-`; when `dirty` is `yes`; when `steps` shows an open, escalated or failed step (run orchestrate-plan, or replan-step); when `reviewed` isn't `current`, because the work changed since its last clean review or never had one (run review-plan-diff); or when `next` is `finish-plan`, because everything is done (run finish-plan).
2. Read the policy from the `landing` line: `integrate` is `direct` or `pull-request`, `release` is `none`, `tag` or `tag+release`, and `changelog` names the changelog file. `draft` is `yes`, which opens the pull request as a draft, or `no`, the default when the Landing section has no `- draft:` line: it stays `no` so that no template update changes how an existing project lands, a project that wants drafts writes `- draft: yes`, and `run-issues` asks for a draft with its extra instructions either way. `follow-ups` is `issues`, which files the plan's follow-ups as issues in this repository, `none`, which files none, or a repository path such as `owner/repo` or `group/subgroup/project`, which files them there. `follow-up-label` names the label filed follow-ups get, in double quotes when it has a space; below, `<label>` is that name without the quotes. `gate` is `none` or the command to run before a push, in double quotes when it has a space; below, `<gate>` is that command without the quotes. `prelude` is `none`, `invalid`, or the PowerShell command that sets up the shell before the gate, such as putting a tool on `PATH`, in double quotes when it has a space; below, `<prelude>` is that command without the quotes. `protect` is `none` or `hook`. `pr-format` is `none` or `<file>#<heading>`, in double quotes when it has a space: a file in the repository and the text of a Markdown heading in it, whose section states this project's pull-request conventions. When it isn't `none`, read that section, from the heading to the next heading of the same or a higher level, and stop when the file or the heading is missing: say to fix the `- pr-format:` line in the `## Landing` section of `AGENTS.md`. Read `PLAN.md`'s title, `Issue:` line, which names one issue or several separated by spaces, Goal, Decisions and `## Follow-ups`, and the state script's `refs` line, which names the issues the plan relates to without resolving them, or `-`. When `release` isn't `none`, stop when `<version>` is `-`, because the plan has no `Release:` line, or when the state script's `changelog-version` isn't `<version>`, because the changelog's newest release section must be this plan's. Stop too when `tag` is `local`: the clone has a `<version>` tag that `origin` doesn't, such as one an older ship-plan left when its push failed. Say to look at it with `git show --no-patch <version>`, delete it with `git tag -d <version>` when nothing else needs it, and run ship-plan again; never push or delete it yourself, because it may point at a commit that never landed or be someone's own tag. Stop when `tag` is `unknown`, because `git ls-remote` couldn't read `origin`'s tags: say to run ship-plan again once `origin` can be reached. When `renumber` isn't `-`, another plan has landed `<version>`, or a later version, since this plan was written, so this plan moves to `<renumber>`. When `pr` is `-`, `CLOSED` or `OPEN`, drop the empty commits as item 5 says, change the `Release:` line of `PLAN.md` to `Release: <renumber>`, and append the step The Renumber Step below gives to the end of its Steps section, numbered in sequence; then stop, and say the release moves to `<renumber>` and that orchestrate-plan, review-plan-diff and ship-plan come next. When `pr` is `OPEN`, also say that the next ship-plan pushes the renumber step to that pull request, which must then merge with a merge commit, not by rebasing. When `tag` is `present`, it must already point at the commit this plan lands; otherwise stop, because a tag is never moved. When `protect` is `hook` and `integrate` is `direct`, stop: the `pre-push` hook refuses a push to `<default>`, so set `integrate: pull-request`. Stop when `draft` is neither `yes` nor `no`: say to set `- draft: yes` or `- draft: no` in the `## Landing` section of `AGENTS.md`. Stop when `follow-ups` is not `issues`, `none` or a repository path with a `/` and no spaces: say to fix the `- follow-ups:` line in the `## Landing` section of `AGENTS.md`. Stop when `prelude` is `invalid`: say to fix the `- prelude:` line in the `## Landing` section of `AGENTS.md`, which must name one command on one line, such as `./build/env.ps1`, a script in the repository that exists, written as `./<path>.ps1`, or `nvs use 26`, without a leading `. ` or `& ` operator, a `#` comment, or `;`, `|`, `&`, `&&` or `||`.
3. With `integrate: direct`, the push to `<default>` must fast-forward, so `behind` matters: when it is more than 0, the default branch moved since the plan branched. Then don't push: drop the empty commits as item 5 says, append a step that merges `origin/<default>` in to the end of the Steps section of `PLAN.md`, numbered in sequence, and stop. The step is the one The Merge Step below gives when the `conflicts` line names files, or the one The Catch-Up Step below gives when it is `none` or `unknown`. Say that the default branch moved, which files conflict, if any, that the step merges `origin/<default>` in, never by rebasing or force-pushing, and that orchestrate-plan, review-plan-diff and ship-plan come next. With `integrate: pull-request`, `behind` alone doesn't matter, because the pull request merges it, but a conflict does: the host can't merge a pull request that conflicts with `<default>`. The `conflicts` line names the files that conflict when `origin/<default>` merges into `HEAD`, separated by `, `, found with `git merge-tree`, which changes no file. When it names files and `pr` is `-`, `CLOSED` or `OPEN`, don't push or open a pull request: drop the empty commits as item 5 says, append the step The Merge Step below gives to the end of the Steps section of `PLAN.md`, numbered in sequence, and stop. Say which files conflict, that the step merges `origin/<default>` in, never by rebasing or force-pushing, and that orchestrate-plan, review-plan-diff and ship-plan come next. When `pr` is `OPEN`, also say that the next ship-plan pushes the step to that pull request, which must then merge with a merge commit, not by rebasing. When `conflicts` is `unknown`, because Git is older than 2.38 or the check failed, go on, and say in the landing summary that the conflict check didn't run. Never merge `origin/<default>` in when `conflicts` is `none` under `integrate: pull-request`: the pull request merges it, and a merge would make the review stale and keep the empty commits.
4. Show the landing summary, then ask me once whether to go ahead and wait for my answer. The summary lists: the commits to land (`git log --oneline origin/<default>..HEAD`), and the empty `Plan:` and `Re-plan step` commits among them that will be dropped; or, when the branch holds a renumber or merge step's merge, that they stay and the pull request must merge with a merge commit, not by rebasing; where they go: the default branch, or a new pull request from `<branch>` and whether it opens as a draft, or, when `pr` is `OPEN`, the open pull request, which takes the commits `git log --oneline origin/<branch>..HEAD` lists; the gate `<gate>` that runs before the push, unless `gate` is `none`, and the prelude `<prelude>` that runs first, in the gate's command, unless `prelude` or `gate` is `none`; the pull request's title and description, when `pr-format` isn't `none`; the tag and the release; what each issue on the `Issue:` line gets, and that each one on the `refs` line gets only a `Refs` line in the pull request description; and each follow-up, which is filed as an issue labelled `<label>`, in this repository or in the one `follow-ups` names, once the plan has landed unless I name it as one to drop. With `follow-ups: none`, say instead that no follow-up is filed, and list them so I can record them where this project tracks its work. After my yes, append ` — dropped` to the line in `PLAN.md` of each follow-up I named, then run every stage below without asking again. `git push` may still ask for its own approval.
5. Drop the empty commits when `landed` is `no` and `origin` has no branch `<branch>` yet, which `git ls-remote --exit-code --heads origin <branch>` shows by exiting 2: `git rebase -f --no-keep-empty (git merge-base HEAD origin/<default>)`. It changes no file, so the review still matches. Ask `origin`, not the branch's upstream: a branch made from `origin/<default>` tracks it before its first push. Skip it when that command exits 0, because the branch is on `origin` and rewriting pushed commits needs a force-push, or exits with another code, because `origin` couldn't say. Skip it too when `pr` is `OPEN`, because the pull request's branch is already pushed. Skip it too when `git rev-list --merges origin/<default>..HEAD` prints a commit, because the rebase would drop the merge a renumber or merge step made.
6. Land the commits, unless `landed` is `yes`: Before the push in any of the first three bullets below, when `gate` isn't `none`, run the gate: run `<gate>; if (-not $? -or $LASTEXITCODE) { exit 1 } else { exit 0 }` in PowerShell from the repository root, with the longest timeout the shell allows, and judge it by its exit code alone, not its output. When `prelude` isn't `none`, the prelude runs first in that same command, dot-sourced so it sets up the shell the gate runs in: `$global:LASTEXITCODE = 0; try { . <prelude> } catch { $_; "prelude failed"; exit 2 }; if (-not $? -or $LASTEXITCODE) { "prelude failed"; exit 2 }; <gate>; if (-not $? -or $LASTEXITCODE) { exit 1 } else { exit 0 }`. When it exits 2, the prelude failed and the gate never ran: stop before pushing, say the prelude failed, show the last 30 lines of its output, and say to fix the `- prelude:` line in the `## Landing` section of `AGENTS.md` or the script it names. When it exits with any other non-zero code, stop before pushing: say the gate failed and show the last 30 lines of its output. When it passes but `git status --porcelain` then prints anything, stop too: the gate changed files, so the review no longer matches what would land.
   - `direct`: when `release` isn't `none` and `tag` is `absent`, tag the commit first: `git tag -a <version> -m <version>`. Then push the commits and the tag together, so both land or neither does: `git push --atomic origin HEAD:refs/heads/<default> refs/tags/<version>`, or `git push origin HEAD:refs/heads/<default>` when there is no tag. When the push fails, such as when it is rejected or not approved, and this run made the tag, the tag must not stay in the clone, where the next run would read `tag` as `present` although `origin` has no such tag: when `git ls-remote --exit-code --tags origin refs/tags/<version>` exits 2, `origin` doesn't have it, so delete it with `git tag -d <version>`; otherwise keep it and say so. A rejected push means the default branch moved since the fetch: stop, and say that the next ship-plan adds the step item 3 gives.
   - `pull-request`, when `pr` is `-` or `CLOSED`: push the branch with `git push -u origin HEAD`, then open the pull request. Its title is the plan's title, and its description is two to five lines summarizing the plan's steps and Decisions. When `pr-format` isn't `none`, write the title and the description as its section says instead, such as a conventional-commit title or required headings, from the plan's title, Goal, steps and Decisions. Either way, the description ends with one `Closes <issue reference>` line for each reference on the plan's `Issue:` line, each on a line of its own, such as `Closes #25` and `Closes #24`. After them come one `Refs <issue reference>` line for each reference on the `refs` line, each on a line of its own, such as `Refs owner/repo#90`, unless the `pr-format` section says where related issues go: then put them there. Before you pass a title or a description to `gh` or `glab`, read it line by line and delete each line of agent attribution, whichever AI agent, assistant or model it names: a `Co-authored-by:` line that names an AI agent or model (Copilot, Claude, Codex, Cursor, Devin, Gemini, Grok, GitLab Duo, aider, a local model or any other) or uses an agent's address, a session trailer such as `Claude-Session:`, `Agent-Logs-Url:` or `Amp-Thread-ID:`, a `Made-with:`, `Assisted-by:` or `Generated-by:` line that names an AI tool, a line that starts, after any symbols or underscores, with words such as "Generated with", "Generated by" or "Created by" and then an AI tool, such as the `_Generated by [Claude Code](…)_` footer a Claude Code cloud session appends, or a line that holds only a link to an agent's session or task, such as a `claude.ai/code/session_` or `chatgpt.com/codex/tasks/` link. The `Commit attribution` check fails a pull request whose title or description holds one, because a merge can copy them into the commit on the default branch. GitHub: `gh pr create --base <default> --head <branch> --title (Get-Content -Raw <title file>).Trim() --body-file <file>`. GitLab, when `host` is `gitlab`: `glab mr create --source-branch <branch> --target-branch <default> --title (Get-Content -Raw <title file>).Trim() --description (Get-Content -Raw <file>) --yes`. When the extra instructions say `draft`, or the `landing` line says `draft=yes`, open it as a draft: add `--draft` to either command.
   - `pull-request`, when `pr` is `OPEN`: when `git rev-list --count origin/<branch>..HEAD` prints more than 0, the branch holds commits the pull request doesn't have yet, such as a renumber or merge step's merge: push them with `git push origin HEAD`, never forced, and say so; when that command fails because `origin` has no `<branch>`, push nothing and say so. When `git rev-list --merges origin/<default>..HEAD` prints a commit, say the pull request must merge with a merge commit, not by rebasing. Then stop here. Say the pull request waits for review and merge, give its URL, and say that running ship-plan again after the merge tags, publishes and closes what's left.
   - `pull-request`, when `pr` is `MERGED`: stop and give the state script's `next`. When the pull request merged into another base branch, as a stacked pull request does, say this branch lands once that branch reaches `<default>`, and to run ship-plan again then. Otherwise it merged without this branch's `HEAD`, because commits were added after it: say to land those commits from a new branch.
7. Tag when `release` isn't `none` and `tag` is still `absent`, as it is after a pull request merged. Tag the commit on the state script's `merge` line, the commit the pull request merged as. When `merge` is `-`, stop and say so: no merged pull request names the commit to tag. Run `git fetch origin`, then `git tag -a <version> -m <version> <commit>` and `git push origin refs/tags/<version>`. When that push fails, remove the tag as item 6's `direct` bullet says, so the next run tags the commit and pushes the tag again.
8. Publish when `release` is `tag+release` and `published` isn't `yes`. Write the changelog's section for `<version>` to a file, without its heading. Its heading is `## [<number>] - <date>`, where `<number>` is `<version>` without a leading `v`, or `## <version>` in a changelog of another format. The section ends at the next `## ` heading or at the link reference definitions that end a Keep a Changelog file. Then on GitHub: `gh release create <version> --verify-tag --title <version> --notes-file <file>`; on GitLab: `glab release create <version> --name <version> --notes-file <file>`.
9. File the follow-ups, unless `follow-ups` is `none`: then skip this stage, and item 12 lists them instead. Below, `<repo args>` is `--repo <owner/repo>` when `follow-ups` names a repository, and nothing when it is `issues`; and `#<number>` is written `<owner/repo>#<number>` for an issue in that repository. Take each line of `## Follow-ups` that doesn't end with `— filed as #<number>`, `— already tracked as #<number>` or `— dropped`. The state script's `unfiled` line counts these lines, and its `next` stays `ship-plan` after the plan has landed until none is left, unless `follow-ups` is `none`. For each:
   - The title is the text before the first `: ` (the first 70 characters of the line when it has none); the rest is the body.
   - Search the open issues for the same work: `gh issue list <repo args> --state open --search (Get-Content -Raw <title file>).Trim() --json number,title --limit 10`, or `glab issue list <repo args> --search (Get-Content -Raw <title file>).Trim() --output json`. When one clearly covers it, file nothing and append ` — already tracked as #<number>` to the line.
   - Make the label once per run, before the first issue: `gh label create "<label>" --color FBCA04 --description "Work a plan found and did not do" <repo args>`, or `glab label create --name "<label>" --color "#FBCA04" --description "Work a plan found and did not do" <repo args>`, where an "already exists" failure is fine and leaves that label as it is. When it fails for another reason, file the issues without `--label "<label>"` and say so.
   - Write the body to a file: the body, a blank line, then `Found while planning <the Issue: references, or the plan's title>; it landed in <the link of the pull request, the release or the commit>.` When `follow-ups` names a repository, write each `Issue:` reference there as the issue's URL, from `gh issue view <number> --json url --jq .url` or the `web_url` of `glab issue view <number> --output json`, because `#<number>` would point into the other repository. Then `gh issue create <repo args> --title (Get-Content -Raw <title file>).Trim() --body-file <file> --label "<label>"`, or `glab issue create <repo args> --title (Get-Content -Raw <title file>).Trim() --description (Get-Content -Raw <file>) --label "<label>"`. Take the number from the URL it prints and append ` — filed as #<number>` to the line in `PLAN.md`, so a second run doesn't file it again.
   - When this run filed any and `issue-state` is `CLOSED`, because the pull request closed its issues, comment once on the first issue on the plan's `Issue:` line, with item 10's comment command: `Follow-ups filed from this plan: #<number> <title>, …`. When `issue-state` is `OPEN`, item 10's comments list them instead.
10. Close the issues when `issue-state` is `OPEN`. The `issue-states` line gives each issue on the `Issue:` line with its state, such as `#25=OPEN #24=CLOSED`: for each one marked `OPEN`, comment once, then close it, one comment per issue. The comment says where the change landed (the release, or the commit or pull request), summarizes the Goal in two to four sentences, names the other issues the plan covered, when it covered several, and lists the follow-ups: each filed one as `#<number> <title>`, and each one marked `— dropped` as plain text, or, with `follow-ups: none`, each one as plain text. GitHub: `gh issue comment <number> --body-file <file>`, then `gh issue close <number>`. GitLab: `glab issue note <number> --message (Get-Content -Raw <file>)`, then `glab issue close <number>`. Add `--repo <owner/repo>` for an issue in another repository. A pull request that merged with `Closes` has already closed its issues, so `issue-state` is `CLOSED` and this stage is skipped. Never comment on or close an issue on the `refs` line: the plan relates to it but doesn't resolve it.
11. Write each title, comment, description, release note and issue body to a temporary file outside the repository with your file-writing tool, in a call of its own, and pass the file to the command; a title goes in as `(Get-Content -Raw <title file>).Trim()`, where the command takes no file. Never put the text in the command line, not even in quotes: a title from `PLAN.md` can come from an issue someone else wrote, and PowerShell expands `$(...)` and backtick sequences inside double quotes. Delete the files in a separate command at the end. A session's own tooling can add agent attribution to what it posts, on GitHub or GitLab, whichever AI agent, assistant or model runs the session: a Claude Code cloud session appends a line `---` and then a footer line `_Generated by [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code/…)_` to each pull request description, issue, comment and review-thread reply it creates, through `gh` and the GitHub MCP tools alike, and other agents, such as Copilot's coding agent, Codex, Cursor, Devin, Jules or GitLab Duo, can append a line of their own that says the text was generated, written or created with or by an AI tool, or a link to the agent's session or task, while `gh` or `glab` in a local session appends nothing. So straight after each command that creates or edits a pull request or merge request description, an issue, or a top-level comment or note, read back what was saved, from the repository it went to. On GitHub: `gh pr view <number> --json body --jq .body` for a pull request, `gh issue view <number> --json body --jq .body` for an issue, each with the `--repo <owner/repo>` the command that posted had, when it had one, or `gh api "repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/comments/<id>" --jq .body` for a comment, where `<owner>/<repo>` is the part of the URL the command printed between `github.com/` and `/issues/` or `/pull/`, and `<id>` is the number after `#issuecomment-` in it. On GitLab: the `description` in what `glab mr view <number> --output json` prints for a merge request or `glab issue view <number> --output json` prints for an issue, each with the `--repo <group/project>` the command that posted had, when it had one, or the `body` in what `glab api "projects/:id/merge_requests/<number>/notes/<id>"` prints for a note, with `issues` in place of `merge_requests` for a note on an issue and, for a note in another project, that project's URL-encoded path, such as `group%2Fproject`, in place of `:id`, where `<id>` is the number after `#note_` in the URL the command printed, or the `id` the API returned. When the last lines of it that aren't blank are agent attribution, each a line that starts, after any symbols or underscores, with words such as `Generated with`, `Generated by`, `Created by` or `Made with` and then an AI tool, agent or model, such as `[Claude Code`, Copilot, Codex, Cursor, Devin, Gemini, Grok or GitLab Duo, or a line that holds only a link to an agent's session or task, such as a `claude.ai/code/session_`, `chatgpt.com/codex/tasks/`, `cursor.com/agents/`, `app.devin.ai/sessions/` or `jules.google.com/task/` link, remove those lines, the `---` line above them, when there is one, and the blank lines between and after them, and keep every other line as it was. Remove it in that same repository, through a route that doesn't append it again. On GitHub, use the GitHub MCP tools when the session has them, because in a Claude Code cloud session an edit through `gh` appends the footer again: `update_pull_request` with the new body for a pull request, `issue_write` with `method: update` and the new body for an issue, or `update_issue_comment` with the comment's id and the new body for a comment; without them, write the new body to a file and run `gh pr edit <number> --body-file <file>`, `gh issue edit <number> --body-file <file>` or `gh api -X PATCH "repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/comments/<id>" -F body=@<file>`, with the same `--repo`. On GitLab, write the new text to a file and run `glab mr update <number> --description (Get-Content -Raw <file>)`, `glab issue update <number> --description (Get-Content -Raw <file>)` or `glab api --method PUT "projects/:id/merge_requests/<number>/notes/<id>" -F body=@<file>`, with the same `--repo`, project and `issues` as the read-back. Then read it back once more; when the attribution is still there, the route appended it again: on GitHub, try the other route once, `gh` after the GitHub MCP tools or the GitHub MCP tools after `gh`, and when it is still there, or there is no other route, as on GitLab, leave it and list it in your report, and for a pull request or merge request description also say that the `Commit attribution` check may fail until a person deletes those lines. Two posts are exceptions. Never edit a `/review` comment, even when it came back with attribution: the `/review` request reads it back itself and deletes it when anything was appended, because NCode Review acts only on the comment as it was created, so an edited `/review` comment requests no review. A reply on a review thread is the other exception: on GitHub nothing a Claude Code cloud session can call edits one without its footer, so post each reply as these instructions say anyway, because every finding still gets its reply, and list the replies in your report as ones that may carry the footer; on GitLab, a reply on a discussion is a note, read back and edited as above with `discussions/<discussion id>/notes/<id>` in place of `notes/<id>`. A session's network can refuse GitHub's GraphQL API, as a Claude Code cloud session's proxy does: then `gh api graphql` and the `gh pr`, `gh issue` and `gh release` commands, which use GraphQL, fail with an error that says GitHub GraphQL is not available, while `gh api` with a REST path still works. After a `gh` command fails that way, run each `gh pr`, `gh issue`, `gh release` and `gh api graphql` command these instructions give in its REST form below for the rest of this run, with `gh api`, and read its answer as that command's: `{owner}/{repo}`, which `gh api` fills in from the clone's `origin`, becomes the `<owner>/<repo>` of the command's `--repo` when it has one, and a body comes from the same file, through `-F body=@<file>`. A list read takes one page at a time, with `&page=<n>` from 1 until a page holds fewer than 100 entries, never `--paginate`, which follows GitHub's next-page links, and those name the repository by a number that the proxy refuses; and a `gh api` command that exits non-zero answers nothing, even when it printed some JSON. `gh pr view <number> --json …` is `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/<number>`: `html_url` is the `url`, `state` is `open` or `closed`, and `MERGED` when `merged` is true, `draft` is `isDraft`, `head.ref` is `headRefName`, `head.sha` is `headRefOid`, `base.ref` is `baseRefName`, `body` is the description, and `isCrossRepository` is true when `head.repo.full_name` differs from `base.repo.full_name`. `gh pr list --state open --search "<number> in:body"` is `gh api "repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls?state=open&per_page=100&page=<n>"`, keeping those whose `body` names the issue. `gh pr create --base <default> --head <branch> --title … --body-file <file>` is `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls -f base=<default> -f head=<branch> -F title=@<title file> -F body=@<file>`, with `-F draft=true` for `--draft`, where the title file holds the title with no line break after it, and its `html_url` and `number` are the new pull request's URL and number. `gh pr edit <number> --body-file <file>` is `gh api -X PATCH repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/<number> -F body=@<file>`. `gh pr comment <number> --body-file <file>` and `gh issue comment <number> --body-file <file>` are `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/<number>/comments -F body=@<file>`, whose `html_url` is the comment's URL, ending in `#issuecomment-<id>`. `gh issue view <number> --json …` is `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/<number>` for its `title`, `body`, `labels`, `state` (`open` or `closed`, which `gh` prints as `OPEN` or `CLOSED`), `assignees` and `html_url`, and `gh api "repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/<number>/comments?per_page=100&page=<n>"` for its comments, each with `user.login`, `body` and `html_url`. `gh issue list --state open …` is `gh api -X GET search/issues -F q=@<query file> -f sort=updated -f order=desc -f per_page=<limit>`, where the query file holds `repo:<owner>/<repo> is:issue is:open <qualifiers>`, and whose `items` are the issues: each `--label <name>` is `label:"<name>"`, `--milestone <title>` is `milestone:"<title>"`, `--assignee <login>` is `assignee:<login>` and `--search <words>` is the words, and without `--repo`, `<owner>/<repo>` is what `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo} --jq .full_name` prints. `gh issue create --title … --body-file <file> --label <label>` is `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues -F title=@<title file> -F body=@<file> -f 'labels[]=<label>'`, `gh issue edit <number> --body-file <file>` is `gh api -X PATCH repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/<number> -F body=@<file>`, and `gh issue close <number>` is `gh api -X PATCH repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/<number> -f state=closed -f state_reason=completed`. `gh release view <tag> --json body --jq .body` is `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/releases/tags/<tag> --jq .body`, and `gh release create <version> --verify-tag --title <version> --notes-file <file>` is `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/git/ref/tags/<version>`, which fails when origin has no such tag, then `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/releases -f tag_name=<version> -f name=<version> -F body=@<file>`. A `gh api graphql` query that reads a pull request's review threads, top-level comments and review summaries is four REST reads, the last three of every page, so a stop for a `hasNextPage` that is `true` doesn't apply: `gh api "repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/<number>/ccr/review_threads"`, the proxy's own route, which answers every thread at once and takes no page, for the threads, each with `resolved` (`isResolved`), `outdated` (`isOutdated`), `path`, `line` and `comment_ids`, the ids of its comments, oldest first; `gh api "repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/<number>/comments?per_page=100&page=<n>"` for those comments, matched by `id`, each with `user.login`, `user.type` (`Bot` for a bot, as `__typename` says), `author_association`, `body` and `html_url`; and `gh api "repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/<number>/comments?per_page=100&page=<n>"` and `gh api "repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/<number>/reviews?per_page=100&page=<n>"` for the top-level comments and the review summaries, with the same fields; the pull request's `state` comes from `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/<number>`, as above. When the threads route fails, read the threads with the GitHub MCP tool `pull_request_read` and its method `get_review_comments` when the session has it, whose threads carry `isResolved`, `isOutdated` and their comments; without it, stop, and say that this session can read no review thread, because GitHub's REST API doesn't say whether a thread is resolved. The `addPullRequestReviewThreadReply` mutation that replies on a thread is `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/<number>/comments/<id>/replies -F body=@<file>`, where `<id>` is the thread's first comment's id, the first of its `comment_ids` or the number after `#discussion_r` in its URL, or the GitHub MCP tool `add_reply_to_pull_request_comment` with that id as `commentId`.
12. Finish with each stage as done, skipped because it was already done, or waiting, the gate as passed or not run, with the links to the pull request, the release and the comment. Run the state script again and give its `next` as the next command: usually `/finish-plan`, which deletes `PLAN.md`, removes the plan's worktree and fast-forwards the default branch. With `follow-ups: none`, list the plan's follow-ups, each line in full, so they can be recorded where this project tracks its work.

## The Renumber Step

Fill in `<changelog>`, `<default>`, `<version>`, `<renumber>`, `<number>` (`<renumber>` without a leading `v`), `<heading>`, `<links>`, `<other-conflicts>` and the step number `<N>`. `<other-conflicts>` covers the files the `conflicts` line names besides `<changelog>`. When it names no other file, or is `none` or `unknown`, `<other-conflicts>` is: When the merge leaves a conflict in any other file, run `git merge --abort` and escalate, naming those files. Otherwise it is: Resolve the conflicts in the other files as these sentences say, keeping every other change from both sides: <resolutions> When a file's sentence says `escalate`, or the merge leaves a conflict in a file not named here, run `git merge --abort` and escalate, naming the file. Write `<resolutions>` as The Merge Step says, for those other files only. When `changelog-format` is `keep-a-changelog`, `<heading>` is `## [<number>] - <date>`, with today's date as `Get-Date -Format yyyy-MM-dd` prints it, and `<links>` is a sentence saying to keep the link reference definitions of `origin/<default>`'s changelog, to change its `[unreleased]` line to compare `<renumber>` with `HEAD`, and to add the `[<number>]` line above the line of `origin/<default>`'s newest version, with both lines written out in full as The Changelog below says. Otherwise `<heading>` is `## <renumber>` and `<links>` is empty:

    ### [ ] <N>. Renumber the release to <renumber>
    - Files: `<changelog>` (edit)
    - Change: another plan landed `<version>` before this one. Run `git merge --no-commit --no-ff origin/<default>`. Then make `<changelog>` hold every section of the changelog on `origin/<default>`, unchanged and in order, with this plan's section above them under the heading `<heading>` instead of its old heading, and no conflict markers. <links> <other-conflicts> Commit note: the merge has already staged the files `origin/<default>` changed, which belong to this step; stage only `<changelog>` and the files this step resolved, and the step's commit records the merge.
    - Done when: `$h = @(Get-Content <changelog> | Where-Object { $_ -match '^## ' -and $_ -notmatch '^## \[Unreleased\]' }); $o = @(git show origin/<default>:<changelog> | Where-Object { $_ -match '^## ' -and $_ -notmatch '^## \[Unreleased\]' }); $t = Get-Content -Raw <changelog>; $in = (git rev-parse -q --verify MERGE_HEAD) -or ((git merge-base HEAD origin/<default>) -eq (git rev-parse origin/<default>)); $links = ($t -notmatch '(?m)^\[unreleased\]:') -or (($t -match '(?m)^\[unreleased\]: \S+/<renumber>\.\.\.HEAD\s*$') -and ($t -match '(?m)^\[<number>\]: \S+<renumber>\s*$')); if ($in -and $links -and -not (git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U) -and $t -notmatch '(?m)^(<<<<<<<|>>>>>>>)' -and $h[0] -match '^## (\[<number>\] - \d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}|v?<number>)$' -and $h[1] -eq $o[0]) { exit 0 } else { exit 1 }`

## The Merge Step

Fill in `<default>`, `<files>`, `<list>`, `<resolutions>` and the step number `<N>`. `<files>` is the files the `conflicts` line names, each in backticks, separated by `, `; `<list>` is the same files, each in single quotes, separated by `, `. `<resolutions>` holds one sentence per file, `` `<file>`: <how to combine the two sides> ``. Write each from the two sides' changes to the file, which `git diff (git merge-base HEAD origin/<default>) origin/<default> -- <file>` and `git diff (git merge-base HEAD origin/<default>) HEAD -- <file>` print: keep both sides' changes, and say exactly how to combine the ones that touch the same lines, such as keeping both new list entries with `<default>`'s first, or giving this plan's new file the next free number and updating the links to it. In the changelog, put both sides' entries of a group under one heading of that group, as The Changelog below says, never under two headings of the same name. When combining them needs a decision that the plan's Decisions don't settle, write `escalate` for that file instead.

    ### [ ] <N>. Merge origin/<default> in
    - Files: <files> (edit)
    - Change: another plan changed these files on `<default>` after this plan branched, so this plan's branch conflicts with it. Run `git merge --no-commit --no-ff origin/<default>`; never rebase. Resolve each file's conflicts as its sentence says, keeping every other change from both sides: <resolutions> When a file's sentence says `escalate`, or the merge leaves a conflict in a file not named here, run `git merge --abort` and escalate, naming the file. Commit note: the merge has already staged the files `origin/<default>` changed, which belong to this step; stage only the files named here, and the step's commit records the merge.
    - Done when: `$in = (git rev-parse -q --verify MERGE_HEAD) -or ((git merge-base HEAD origin/<default>) -eq (git rev-parse origin/<default>)); $marks = @(Select-String -LiteralPath <list> -Pattern '^(<<<<<<<|>>>>>>>)( |$)' -ErrorAction Ignore); if ($in -and -not (git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U) -and $marks.Count -eq 0) { exit 0 } else { exit 1 }`

## The Catch-Up Step

Fill in `<default>` and the step number `<N>`.

    ### [ ] <N>. Merge origin/<default> in
    - Files: none; the merge brings in the commits `<default>` gained after this plan branched
    - Change: `<default>` moved after this plan branched, and the push to it must fast-forward. Run `git merge --no-commit --no-ff origin/<default>`; never rebase. When the merge leaves a conflict in any file, run `git merge --abort` and escalate, naming the files. Commit note: the merge has already staged the files `origin/<default>` changed, which belong to this step; stage nothing else, and the step's commit records the merge.
    - Done when: `$in = (git rev-parse -q --verify MERGE_HEAD) -or ((git merge-base HEAD origin/<default>) -eq (git rev-parse origin/<default>)); if ($in -and -not (git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U)) { exit 0 } else { exit 1 }`

## The Changelog

The changelog is the file the `changelog` key of `AGENTS.md`'s `## Landing` section names, `CHANGELOG.md` by default. Read it before you write its step. It follows Keep a Changelog 1.1.0 (https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/) when it has a `## [Unreleased]` heading or a heading such as `## [1.4.0] - 2026-10-28`. The state script prints `changelog-format: keep-a-changelog` for such a file, `other` for a changelog in any other format, and `missing` when there is no file.

A Keep a Changelog file holds, in order: `# Changelog`, its preamble, `## [Unreleased]`, one `## [<number>] - <date>` section per release, newest first, and the link reference definitions. `<number>` is the version without a leading `v` (`1.4.0` for `v1.4.0`). `<date>` is the day the section is written, as `Get-Date -Format yyyy-MM-dd` prints it. A section's entries are `- ` bullets written for the project's users. An entry for a change that breaks how existing users work starts with `**Breaking:**` and says what to change; an entry ends with a link to the issue it closes and, when one records the decision, its decision record, such as `([#42](<web>/issues/42), [ADR-1007](docs/decisions/1007-<title>.md))`; and a dependency update that closes a vulnerability names its advisory, such as `GHSA-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx` or the CVE, under `### Security`. They are grouped under these headings, in this order, and each heading appears only when it has an entry: `### Added` (new commands, files, settings, options or output), `### Changed` (changes to behavior or documentation), `### Deprecated`, `### Removed`, `### Fixed` (behavior that was wrong) and `### Security` (a vulnerability or exposure closed). A section has at most one of each heading: an entry goes under its group's heading when the section already has it, and is never put under a second heading of the same name, also when two sides' changes to the changelog are combined. Two pull requests that each add the same heading to `## [Unreleased]` merge without a conflict and leave the heading twice; the state script names each heading a section has more than once as `changelog-duplicates: <section> <heading>`, such as `[Unreleased] Changed`, joined by `, `, or prints `-`. The link reference definitions come newest first. The first is `[unreleased]: <web>/compare/<newest tag>...HEAD`. Then each release has `[<number>]: <web>/compare/<previous tag>...<tag>`, or `[<number>]: <web>/releases/tag/<tag>` for the first release. `<web>` is the repository's web address: `git remote get-url origin` written as `https://<host>/<path>` without `.git`. On GitLab, the links use `<web>/-/compare/` and `<web>/-/tags/<tag>`. Tags keep the project's prefix, such as `v1.4.0`. A file with no release yet has no link reference definitions.

The plan's last step writes the plan's entries, for every plan:

- `missing`: create the file, then write to it as for `keep-a-changelog`. It starts with these lines, each followed by a blank line except the last: `# Changelog`, then `All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.`, then `The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/), and this project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html).`, then `## [Unreleased]`.
- `keep-a-changelog`, without a `Release:` line: add the entries under `## [Unreleased]`, putting each in its group, and add to a group that is already there instead of writing its heading again. When `changelog-duplicates` names a heading of `[Unreleased]`, the step also merges that heading's groups into one, at the first one's place, keeping every entry in order.
- `keep-a-changelog`, with a `Release:` line: insert `## [<number>] - <date>` right below `## [Unreleased]`. Put in it every entry `## [Unreleased]` held and the plan's own, in one set of groups with each heading once, and leave `## [Unreleased]` empty. Set the `[unreleased]` link to compare the new tag with `HEAD`, and add the new version's link above the previous version's.
- `other`, with a `Release:` line: add that version's section at the top, in the style of the sections below it.
- `other`, without a `Release:` line: leave the file as it is.

Write the step so the executor copies text: it gives the heading, each entry under its group, and each link line in full. Only `<date>` is left to the executor, with the `Get-Date` command. Never reformat a changelog in another format, or an older section of any changelog, unless the request asks for it, as an adopted project's follow-up does; a heading that `changelog-duplicates` names in an older release section stays as it is. A plan that converts a changelog keeps every entry's text. It dates each version's heading with its tag's date (`git log -1 --format=%as <tag>`), puts each entry in one group, and adds the preamble, `## [Unreleased]` and the link reference definitions.

A project can have version tags its changelog has no section for, such as the releases it made before a plan first created the changelog. They are the tags `git tag --list --merged HEAD` prints that are shaped like `v1.2.3` or `1.2.3` and match no release heading in the changelog, such as `## [1.2.3] - <date>` or `## v1.2.3`. The state script prints them as `changelog-backfill: <oldest>..<newest>`, as the tag alone when there is one, or as `-` when there is none, and `Update-Project.ps1` and the template's `Adopt-Project.ps1` print a request to backfill them. When there are any, and the plan isn't that backfill, list this follow-up under `## Follow-ups`, filling in `<changelog>` and `<range>`: `Backfill the changelog from past releases: add a section to <changelog> for each version tag in <range> that has none, from the tag's release notes, so the changelog covers the project's full release history.` A backfill plan writes one `## [<number>] - <date>` section for each such tag, dated with the tag's date (`git log -1 --format=%as <tag>`) and placed among the other sections by version, newest first; in a changelog of another format, it writes it in the style of the sections there. The planning session fetches each tag's release notes, with `gh release view <tag> --json body --jq .body` on GitHub or `glab release view <tag>` on GitLab, and copies the entries into the plan's steps, because the executor never calls `gh` or `glab`. For a tag without a release, it summarizes `git log --oneline <previous tag>..<tag>`, or `git log --oneline <tag>` for the first tag, into entries for the project's users. It puts each entry in one group and keeps the project's own marker for a breaking change, such as a `**Breaking:**` prefix. It adds each version's link line in order, and the `[unreleased]` link when the file has none; a changelog of another format gets no links. A backfill of many tags spreads them over several steps, a few versions each.
